title: Hybrid Cloud: Private Data, Public Front End
description: When sensitive data stays on premises and a scalable web front end runs in the public cloud, the model is hybrid. Network+ N10-009 objective 1.3.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 1, Networking concepts, which is 23 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 1 point 3. Summarize cloud concepts and connectivity options. Let's pick the right deployment model for a split workload. A company must keep sensitive data on premises, but wants its web front end to scale in the cloud. One side is private. The other is public cloud. A connection joins them into one deployment. That is hybrid. Private alone has no public half, and public alone has no on-premises half. When a scenario keeps sensitive data on premises and runs a scalable front end in the public cloud, the answer is hybrid. Private alone, or public alone, only describes half. That's objective one point three.

title: What Lets a VPC Reach the Internet? The Internet Gateway
description: An internet gateway is the cloud component that lets a VPC exchange traffic with the internet. Network+ N10-009 objective 1.3.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 1, Networking concepts, which is 23 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 1 point 3. Summarize cloud concepts and connectivity options. Today: how does a virtual private cloud actually reach the internet? A virtual private cloud, or V P C, is your own isolated network inside the provider's cloud. By default, the instances inside have no path to the internet. The component that fixes that is the internet gateway. It attaches to the V P C and connects it to the internet, and the subnet needs a route that points to it. Traffic now flows both ways between the V P C and the internet, through the internet gateway. When the question asks which cloud component lets a V P C exchange traffic with the internet, the answer is the internet gateway. That's objective one point three.

title: 10 Gb/s Between 100 and 500 Meters: Multimode Fiber
description: Why multimode fiber is the right cable for 10 Gb/s over more than 100 meters but under 500 meters. Network+ N10-009 objective 1.5.
takeaway: Over 100 m and under 500 m at 10 Gb/s: multimode fiber
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 1, Networking concepts, which is 23 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 1 point 5. Compare and contrast transmission media and transceivers. Today's concept: matching the cable to the distance. The question is a distance problem. You need ten gigabits per second, over more than one hundred meters, but less than five hundred. Copper, even Cat six A, tops out at one hundred meters. Multimode fiber, O M three and O M four, carries ten gigabit roughly three hundred to four hundred meters, and costs less than single-mode. Our target zone starts where copper ends. Multimode fiber covers it at the lowest sensible cost. Remember the pattern. Copper stops at one hundred meters. For ten gigabit past that and under five hundred, pick multimode fiber. Single-mode works, but costs more. That's objective one point five.

title: DSL: Why Speed Drops With Distance
description: DSL runs over telephone lines and slows as distance from the provider's equipment grows. Network+ N10-009 objective 1.6.
takeaway: Telephone lines + speed falls with distance = DSL
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 1, Networking concepts, which is 23 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 1 point 6. Compare and contrast network topologies, architectures, and types. Under provider links, there's one that depends on how far away you are. D S L delivers internet over ordinary telephone lines. The farther your home or office is from the provider's equipment, the weaker the signal, and the slower the connection. Distance goes up, speed goes down. That is the signature of D S L. If a question mentions telephone lines and speed that drops with distance from the provider, the answer is D S L. That's objective one point six.

title: SD-WAN Local Breakout: Skip the Headquarters Detour
description: With local breakout an SD-WAN edge sends trusted cloud application traffic straight out of the branch instead of through headquarters. Network+ N10-009 objective 1.8.
takeaway: Local breakout = app traffic goes direct, not via HQ
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 1, Networking concepts, which is 23 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 1 point 8. Summarize evolving use cases for modern network environments. Today's concept: why a branch user's email goes straight to the cloud in an SD-WAN. A branch office, a headquarters, and a cloud email service. The old way sent everything to headquarters first, and then out to the cloud. That detour is called hairpinning, and it adds delay. With SD-WAN local breakout, the branch edge device recognizes the application and sends trusted cloud traffic straight to the nearest service. DHCP is not the reason. It only gives out an address and a default gateway. It does not choose a path per application. For the exam, when branch cloud traffic skips headquarters, the answer is local breakout, driven by application-aware policy. DHCP only hands out addresses and a gateway. That's objective one point eight.

title: SDN: Control, Data and Management Planes
description: The control plane builds routing and switching tables, the data plane forwards packets, and the management plane is how you configure the device. SDN centralizes the control plane. Network+ N10-009 1.8.
takeaway: Control plane builds tables, data plane forwards
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 1, Networking concepts, which is 23 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 1 point 8. Summarize evolving use cases for modern network environments. Today's concept: the three planes of a network device, and which one builds the tables. Every router and switch does three jobs. Each job is called a plane. The management plane is how you configure the device, for example over SSH or SNMP. The control plane is the brain. It builds the routing table and the switching table. The data plane does the work. For every packet it looks up the table and forwards it. It never builds the table itself. A common mistake is to say management plane, because you configure things there. But configuring is not building the tables. In software-defined networking, the control plane moves into one central controller. The controller pushes forwarding rules down to the switches. The switches keep only the data plane. On the exam, ask who builds the routing and switching tables. That is the control plane. The data plane only forwards, and the management plane is how you configure the device. That's objective one point eight.

title: SSE vs SASE, and What a VTEP Does
description: SSE bundles SWG, CASB, ZTNA and FWaaS; SASE is SSE plus SD-WAN. A VTEP adds and removes VXLAN encapsulation. Network+ N10-009 objective 1.8.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 1, Networking concepts, which is 23 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 1 point 8. Summarize evolving use cases for modern network environments. Today's concept: SSE versus SASE, and the job of a VTEP. Security service edge, or SSE, is a bundle of cloud-delivered security services. It combines a secure web gateway, a cloud access security broker, zero trust network access, and firewall as a service. Add SD-WAN to that security bundle and you have secure access service edge, or SASE. One part worth remembering: the cloud access security broker controls software as a service use and finds shadow IT. A VXLAN tunnel endpoint, or VTEP, sits at each end of a VXLAN tunnel. Its job is to add the VXLAN encapsulation as frames go into the tunnel, and remove it as they come out. For the exam, SSE is the security bundle, and SASE is SSE plus SD-WAN. A VTEP is the edge device that adds and removes the VXLAN wrapper. That's objective one point eight.

title: VXLAN: UDP Port 4789 and the 24-Bit VNI
description: VXLAN wraps a Layer 2 frame in UDP port 4789 and tags it with a 24-bit VNI, about 16 million segments versus 4,094 usable VLANs. Network+ N10-009 objective 1.8.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 1, Networking concepts, which is 23 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 1 point 8. Summarize evolving use cases for modern network environments. Today's concept: the two numbers to remember for VXLAN. Two virtual machines sit in different racks, with a routed IP network between them. They need to behave as if they share one Layer 2 network. So VXLAN takes the original Ethernet frame and wraps it. The wrapper is a UDP packet addressed to port four seven eight nine, plus a VXLAN header that carries the VNI, the virtual network identifier. A VLAN ID has twelve bits, so about four thousand segments. The VNI has twenty four bits, which is more than sixteen million segments. If an answer offers five oh six oh, that is the SIP voice port. VXLAN is four seven eight nine. For the exam, VXLAN means UDP port four seven eight nine and a twenty four bit VNI. Five oh six oh is the port for SIP voice, and a VLAN ID is only twelve bits. That's objective one point eight.

title: Administrative Distance Is Compared Before Metric
description: A router compares administrative distance first and installs the lowest. Metrics only choose between routes from the same source. Network+ N10-009 objective 2.1.
takeaway: Lowest AD wins · metric only breaks ties
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 2, Network implementation, which is 20 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 2 point 1. Explain characteristics of routing technologies. Today's concept: when two routes disagree, what does the router compare first? A router learns a default route two ways. One is typed in by an administrator, a static route. The other is learned from RIP. RIP shows a lower metric, just one hop. That tempts people to choose RIP. But the router does not compare those numbers first. First it compares administrative distance, which measures how much the router trusts the source. Static is one. RIP is one hundred twenty. One is lower than one hundred twenty, so the static route is installed. The decision is made before the metric is ever looked at. Metric only matters when two routes come from the same protocol, such as two RIP paths with one hop and three hops. For the exam, administrative distance decides between route sources, and the lowest one wins. Metric is only used to choose among routes from the same protocol. That's objective two point one.

title: GLBP: First Hop Redundancy With Load Balancing
description: GLBP is the first hop redundancy protocol that can spread client traffic across several gateways at once, unlike HSRP and VRRP. Network+ N10-009 objective 2.1.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 2, Network implementation, which is 20 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 2 point 1. Explain characteristics of routing technologies. Inside it, first hop redundancy protocols. Which one can share the load? Three clients share two gateways for redundancy. With H S R P or V R R P, one router is active, or master, and carries all the traffic. The other waits as a standby. G L B P, which is Cisco proprietary, changes that. It hands out different gateways to different clients, so both routers forward traffic at the same time. HSRP and VRRP normally send everything through one active router. G L B P adds load balancing across the gateways. That's objective two point one.

title: Roaming: The BSSID Changes, the ESSID Stays
description: When a client roams between access points in one wireless network, the BSSID of the access point changes while the ESSID, the network name, stays the same. Network+ N10-009 objective 2.3.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 2, Network implementation, which is 20 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 2 point 3. Given a scenario, select and configure wireless devices and technologies. Today's concept: what changes, and what does not, when a user roams between access points. Two access points broadcast the same network name, Office. That shared name is the ESSID. But each access point radio has its own hardware address, the BSSID. A user sits near the first access point. The laptop is associated with BSSID zero one. The user walks across the building. The laptop moves to the second access point. The BSSID changed from zero one to zero two. The ESSID stayed Office, so the user notices nothing. For the exam, the network name is the ESSID, and it stays the same while you roam. The BSSID identifies each access point's radio, so it changes. That's objective two point three.

title: Wi-Fi 6, 6E and 7: Which Is Which?
description: 802.11ax is Wi-Fi 6 on 2.4 and 5 GHz, Wi-Fi 6E adds the 6 GHz band, and 802.11be is Wi-Fi 7 with multi-link operation. Network+ N10-009 objective 2.3.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 2, Network implementation, which is 20 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 2 point 3. Given a scenario, select and configure wireless devices and technologies. Today's concept: matching Wi-Fi generations to standards, bands and features. Here are the recent generations, from Wi-Fi four to Wi-Fi seven. Each has an IEEE standard behind it. Eight oh two dot eleven N, A C, A X, and B E. Wi-Fi six uses the two point four and five gigahertz bands. Wi-Fi six E is the same standard, extended into the six gigahertz band. Wi-Fi seven uses all three. Two features separate them. BSS coloring is a Wi-Fi six feature, it tags frames so an access point can ignore a neighbor on the same channel. Multi-link operation arrives with Wi-Fi seven. So ax is Wi-Fi six, not seven. And five gigahertz is not the new band. The new band is six gigahertz. For the exam, eight oh two dot eleven A X is Wi-Fi six. Six E adds the six gigahertz band. Eight oh two dot eleven B E is Wi-Fi seven, and it brings multi-link operation. That's objective two point three.

title: Wi-Fi Channels 1, 6 and 11, and Interference Types
description: In 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6 and 11 avoid overlapping. Co-channel interference shares airtime; adjacent-channel interference corrupts frames. Network+ N10-009 objective 2.3.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 2, Network implementation, which is 20 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 2 point 3. Given a scenario, select and configure wireless devices and technologies. Today's concept: the non-overlapping 2.4 gigahertz channels, and the two kinds of channel interference. The 2.4 gigahertz band is crowded. Channels are only five megahertz apart, but each one is about twenty megahertz wide, so most of them overlap. The three channels that do not overlap are one, six and eleven. Use those for neighbouring access points. Two things can go wrong. Co-channel interference is two access points on the same channel. They hear each other and take turns, so airtime is shared. Adjacent channel interference is worse. The channels overlap only partly, so the devices cannot decode each other and do not take turns. The frames just get corrupted. For the exam, in 2.4 gigahertz the clean channels are one, six and eleven. Two access points on the same channel take turns, which is co-channel interference. Overlapping channels corrupt each other, and that adjacent channel interference is worse. That's objective two point three.

title: Twisted-Pair Ethernet: The 100 Meter Channel Limit
description: The maximum channel length for twisted-pair Ethernet is 100 meters: 90 meters of permanent link plus patch cords. Network+ N10-009 objective 2.4.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 2, Network implementation, which is 20 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 2 point 4. Explain important factors of physical installations. Start with the number every installer memorizes: the twisted pair distance limit. Twisted pair Ethernet has a hard distance limit. Here is how it adds up. Ninety meters of permanent link, the run from the wall jack to the patch panel. Plus up to ten meters of patch cords in total, for both ends. Together that's a one hundred meter channel. Not fifty-five. One hundred. The channel limit for twisted pair Ethernet is one hundred meters: ninety of permanent link, plus the patch cords. That's objective two point four.

title: End of Life vs. End of Support
description: A vendor stops providing security patches for a router. That milestone is end of support, not end of life. Network+ N10-009 objective 3.1.
takeaway: No more patches or help = end of support
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 3, Network operations, which is 19 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 3 point 1. Explain the purpose of organizational processes and procedures. Two milestones sound alike, and the exam likes to swap them. Picture a product's life as a timeline. It starts out in service. At end of life, the vendor stops selling it. Later comes end of support: no more security patches, and no more help. In the question, a vendor stops providing security patches for a router. That's the last milestone, end of support. When the question says the vendor no longer provides patches or help, the answer is end of support. End of life comes earlier, when the product stops being sold. That's objective three point one.

title: Zero RPO Requires Synchronous Replication
description: RPO measures how much data you can lose. A zero RPO accepts no data loss, so writes must be replicated synchronously. Network+ N10-009 objective 3.3.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 3, Network operations, which is 19 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 3 point 3. Explain disaster-recovery concepts. Today: which recovery point objective needs synchronous replication? R P O stands for recovery point objective. It is how much data you can afford to lose, measured back from the failure. The gap between the last good copy and the failure is the data you lose. To make that gap zero, every write must reach the replica before it counts as done. That's synchronous replication. A zero R P O accepts no data loss, so it requires it. Lock this in. R P O is how much data loss you can accept. Zero means none, and the only way to get zero is to replicate every write synchronously. That's objective three point three.

title: What Is Out-of-Band Management?
description: Out-of-band management reaches a device over a separate dedicated path that still works when the production network is down. Network+ N10-009 objective 3.5.
takeaway: Out-of-band = a separate, dedicated management path
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 3, Network operations, which is 19 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 3 point 5. Compare and contrast network access and management methods. Today's concept is out-of-band management. Normally an admin manages a switch over the same production network that carries everyone's traffic. That's in-band. Out-of-band adds a second, dedicated path, like a console server, that does not depend on production. Independence is the test. A management VLAN on the production switches is still in-band. Now the production network fails. The in-band path is gone. But the admin can still reach the switch, because the dedicated path never touched production. For the exam, out-of-band means a dedicated path that is independent of production. If the network is down and you can still manage the device, that's out-of-band. That's objective three point five.

title: TACACS+ Uses TCP 49, RADIUS Uses UDP 1812
description: TACACS+ runs over TCP port 49, while RADIUS authentication uses UDP port 1812. Network+ N10-009 objective 4.1.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 4, Network security, which is 14 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 4 point 1. Explain the importance of basic network security concepts. Today's concept: the transport and port for TACACS plus, and how it differs from RADIUS. A network device sends logins to an AAA server. Two common choices are TACACS plus and RADIUS. TACACS plus travels over TCP, port forty nine. RADIUS travels over UDP. Port eighteen twelve carries authentication, and port eighteen thirteen carries accounting. The common mix-up is to pair TACACS plus with UDP eighteen twelve. That port belongs to RADIUS. A simple hook: T for TCP, T for TACACS plus. TACACS plus also protects the whole packet body, while RADIUS hides only the password. For the exam, TACACS plus is T for TCP, port forty nine. RADIUS is UDP, with eighteen twelve for authentication and eighteen thirteen for accounting. That's objective four point one.

title: ACL Rules Run Top Down, First Match Wins
description: An ACL is checked from the top down and the first matching rule wins; traffic that matches nothing hits the implicit deny. Network+ N10-009 objective 4.3.
takeaway: Top down · first match wins · implicit deny at the end
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 4, Network security, which is 14 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 4 point 3. Given a scenario, apply network security features, defense techniques, and solutions. Today's concept: the order in which an access control list is evaluated. An access control list is a numbered set of rules. The device reads them from the top down. A packet from host ten dot one dot one dot five arrives. It is compared with rule one first. It matches rule one, so it is denied. The first match wins, and rule two is never even looked at. That is why order matters. If the broad permit were first, host five would be allowed through, and the deny would never run. If a packet matches no rule at all, it falls off the end. Every list finishes with an implicit deny, so the packet is dropped. For the exam, an access control list is read from the top down, and the first rule that matches decides. If nothing matches, the implicit deny at the end drops the packet. That's objective four point three.

title: DNSSEC Does Not Hide Your DNS Queries
description: DNSSEC proves who sent a DNS answer and that it was not changed, but it does not encrypt the lookup. Network+ N10-009 objective 4.3.
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 4, Network security, which is 14 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 4 point 3. Given a scenario, apply network security features, defense techniques, and solutions. Today's concept: what DNSSEC actually protects, and what it does not. Here a client looks up a name from a zone that is validly signed. The answer comes back with a signature. The client checks the chain of trust, and it can be sure the data came from the right zone and was not changed on the way. But look at the question itself. It still travels in the clear. Anyone watching the wire can read it. So an analyst who says the lookup is now hidden needs a correction. DNSSEC validates origin and integrity. Confidentiality is a different problem. On the exam, when you see DNSSEC, think origin and integrity. If the question asks about hiding the lookup, that needs a separate mechanism like DNS over HTTPS or TLS. That's objective four point three.

title: Straight-Through Cable Between Two Switches Without Auto-MDIX
description: Two older switches without Auto-MDIX joined by a straight-through cable have no link, because transmit meets transmit. Network+ N10-009 objective 5.2.
takeaway: Like devices + straight-through cable = TX meets TX = no link
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 5, Network troubleshooting, which is 24 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 5 point 2. Given a scenario, troubleshoot common cabling and physical interface issues. Today's symptom: a link that stays down because transmit and receive are on the wrong pins. Two older switches, no Auto M D I X, connected with a straight-through cable. Switch ports are M D I X. They transmit on pins three and six, and receive on one and two. A straight-through cable keeps the pins in the same order end to end. So both sides transmit on the same pair, and neither one listens. Transmit meets transmit. No link. Auto M D I X, or a crossover cable, swaps the pairs, so transmit finally meets receive. For the exam, two older switches joined by a straight-through cable, with no Auto M D I X, give you no link, because transmit meets transmit. A crossover cable or Auto M D I X fixes it. That's objective five point two.

title: Got a DHCP Address But Can't Reach Neighbors: Check the VLAN
description: A device that gets a DHCP address but cannot reach neighbors on the same switch is often in the wrong VLAN. Check the switch port's VLAN first. Network+ N10-009 objective 5.3.
takeaway: Has an IP but can't reach neighbors: check the port's VLAN
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 5, Network troubleshooting, which is 24 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 5 point 3. Given a scenario, troubleshoot common issues with network services. Here's a classic scenario. The device has an address, but nothing works. Three PCs on one switch. A and B work together fine. PC C got an address by D H C P, but it can't reach its neighbors. Notice its port sits in a different VLAN, so it landed on a different network. The port's VLAN decides the subnet, and the subnet decides who you can reach. So check the VLAN on the switch port first. Move the port into the right VLAN and the problem goes away. When a device gets a DHCP address but can't talk to neighbors that work fine, check the V LAN assigned to its switch port first. That's objective five point three.

title: ip addr, ipconfig and tracert: Which OS, Which Job?
description: On modern Linux, ip addr shows IP address information. ipconfig is the Windows equivalent, and tracert traces a path rather than showing an address. Network+ N10-009 objective 5.5.
takeaway: Show my IP: ip addr (Linux) · ipconfig (Windows)
transcript: CompTIA Network Plus, domain 5, Network troubleshooting, which is 24 percent of the exam. This lesson covers objective 5 point 5. Given a scenario, use the appropriate tool or protocol to solve networking issues. Today's concept: three commands that look alike, and which operating system and job each belongs to. Two jobs, two operating systems. The first job is showing your own IP address information. The second is tracing the path to another host. On modern Linux, ip addr shows the address. On Windows, the command is ipconfig. Linux still has the older ifconfig, but ip is the modern tool. For tracing, Linux uses traceroute and Windows uses tracert. So tracert is the wrong answer for a question about address information. It lists the routers along a path. It does not show your own address. For the exam, to see IP address information on modern Linux, use IP space ADDR. Ipconfig is Windows. And tracert traces a path, it does not show your address. That's objective five point five.
